(29.81%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
This case highlights the importance of recognizing and evaluating potential vascular injury in the context of a clavicular fracture. When clinical signs suggest vascular compromise (diminished pulses, pallor, coolness), immediate vascular assessment with Doppler ultrasound is essential to identify subclavian artery injury and prevent limb-threatening complications. Early recognition and management of vascular injury takes priority over fracture management.
(Choice A)
MRI of the shoulder
MRI is not indicated for initial evaluation of clavicle fractures or suspected vascular injury. Plain radiographs are sufficient for fracture assessment, and vascular evaluation requires Doppler ultrasound or CT angiography.
(Choice B)
Ultrasound of the upper extremity
While ultrasound can assess vascular flow, a focused Doppler study by vascular specialists is more appropriate when there are clinical signs of vascular compromise.
(Choice C)
Immediate orthopedic referral for fracture reduction
While orthopedic consultation will ultimately be needed for fracture management, vascular assessment takes priority when there are signs of vascular compromise such as diminished pulses or poor perfusion.
(Choice D)
Vascular consult for Doppler ultrasound
It's important to assess vascular integrity via Doppler, especially when there’s suspicion of vascular injury.
(Choice E)
Neurophysiological assessment of the upper limb
Neurological assessment focuses on nerve function rather than vascular integrity. While brachial plexus injury can occur with clavicle fractures, the clinical signs described suggest vascular rather than neurological compromise.

pages.question: A 72-year-old man with a history of hip fracture repair 3 weeks ago is referred to a wound care clinic for a non-healing sacral pressure ulcer (stage III, 6 cm × 5 cm) that developed during his hospitalization. He is now in a skilled nursing facility where he receives a standard hospital diet. His weight is 58 kg (usual weight 71 kg — a 12-kg loss over 4 months), and his BMI is 19.1 kg/m². Laboratory values show albumin 2.6 g/dL, prealbumin 9 mg/dL, CRP 42 mg/L, zinc 48 µg/dL (normal 60–120 µg/dL). His wound shows minimal granulation tissue, no signs of infection, and no epithelialization at the edges. You are asked to recommend nutritional interventions to optimize wound healing. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate comprehensive nutritional strategy for this patient?

answers.text:
Increase dietary fat to 40% of total calories as the primary intervention to improve caloric density
(0%)

Supplement with vitamin C alone at 1000 mg/day
(0%)

Initiate total parenteral nutrition immediately to bypass gastrointestinal absorption issues
(0%)

High-protein oral nutritional supplementation with arginine, vitamin C, and zinc supplementation
(100%)

Continue the standard hospital diet and reassess wound status in 4 weeks
(0%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
Malnourished patients with pressure ulcers require comprehensive multimodal nutritional support including high-protein intake (1.5–2.0 g/kg/day), supplemental arginine (which promotes nitric oxide-mediated tissue perfusion and serves as a collagen precursor), vitamin C (500–1000 mg/day for collagen hydroxylation and cross-linking), and zinc supplementation (to correct deficiency and support metalloproteinase-mediated remodeling). Standard hospital diets are inadequate to meet the elevated metabolic demands of wound healing in malnourished patients with large pressure ulcers.
(Choice A)
Increase dietary fat to 40% of total calories as the primary intervention to improve caloric density
While adequate total caloric intake is important to prevent protein from being used as an energy source (thereby sparing it for anabolic functions including wound repair), simply increasing dietary fat does not address the specific deficiencies driving impaired wound healing in this patient. The critical interventions are protein repletion and targeted micronutrient supplementation (arginine, vitamin C, zinc). A fat-heavy diet without attention to protein and micronutrients would fail to optimize the wound healing milieu.
(Choice B)
Supplement with vitamin C alone at 1000 mg/day
Vitamin C supplementation addresses only one component of the wound healing deficit in this patient. While vitamin C is critical for collagen hydroxylation and cross-linking, this patient also has severe protein-calorie malnutrition, zinc deficiency, and likely arginine insufficiency — none of which are addressed by vitamin C alone. A comprehensive, multimodal nutritional strategy is required to meet the elevated metabolic demands of wound healing in a malnourished patient with a large pressure ulcer.
(Choice C)
Initiate total parenteral nutrition immediately to bypass gastrointestinal absorption issues
TPN is indicated only when the gastrointestinal tract is non-functional or inaccessible. This patient shows no evidence of gastrointestinal dysfunction and can tolerate oral nutrition. Enteral nutrition (oral or tube feeding) is always preferred over TPN when the GI tract is functional because it preserves gut mucosal integrity, reduces infection risk, and avoids TPN-associated complications including catheter-related bloodstream infections, metabolic derangements, and hepatic dysfunction. TPN would be unnecessarily invasive and inappropriate as a first-line intervention.
(Choice D)
High-protein oral nutritional supplementation with arginine, vitamin C, and zinc supplementation
This patient has significant protein-calorie malnutrition (18% unintentional weight loss, albumin 2.6 g/dL, prealbumin 9 mg/dL) combined with documented zinc deficiency (48 µg/dL), all of which impair the wound healing cascade at multiple levels. Protein at 1.5–2.0 g/kg/day (87–116 g/day for this 58-kg patient) provides amino acid substrates for fibroblast proliferation, collagen triple helix formation, and immune cell function. Arginine supplementation (4.5–15 g/day) is particularly important in wound healing: as a substrate for nitric oxide synthase, arginine enhances local microvascular perfusion at the wound bed and serves as a direct precursor for proline (via the arginine-to-ornithine-to-proline pathway), directly fueling collagen synthesis. Vitamin C supplementation (500–1000 mg/day) restores hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues, which is critical for collagen cross-linking and tensile strength. Zinc supplementation (40–50 mg/day elemental zinc) addresses the documented deficiency and supports metalloproteinase activity needed for wound remodeling and epithelial cell migration. Disease-specific oral nutritional supplements (e.g., Arginaid, Juven) are commercially available and evidence-supported for pressure ulcer management in malnourished patients per NPUAP/EPUAP guidelines.
(Choice E)
Continue the standard hospital diet and reassess wound status in 4 weeks
Continuing a standard hospital diet is insufficient for a patient with severe protein-calorie malnutrition (albumin 2.6 g/dL, prealbumin 9 mg/dL, 18% unintentional weight loss) and a large stage III pressure ulcer. Standard hospital diets typically provide only 0.8 g/kg/day of protein, well below the 1.5–2.0 g/kg/day needed for wound healing in malnourished patients. This patient requires immediate aggressive nutritional intervention - delaying for 4 weeks would likely result in wound deterioration and increased complications.

pages.question: A 56-year-old male with a history of long-standing dyspepsia returns to the clinic presenting with recurring episodes of black tarry stools and dizziness. He mentions that he hasn't been consistent with his prescribed proton pump inhibitors. Considering the patient's symptoms and history, what is the most common complication associated with untreated peptic ulcer disease?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
Gastrointestinal bleeding, manifested as hematemesis or melena, is the most common complication of peptic ulcer disease, affecting 15-20% of patients. It requires prompt hemodynamic assessment, resuscitation if needed, and often urgent upper endoscopy for diagnosis and potential therapeutic intervention. While perforation, penetration, and gastric outlet obstruction are serious complications, they occur with significantly lower frequency.
(Choice A)
Gastrointestinal bleeding
Gastrointestinal bleeding is the most common and severe complication of peptic ulcer disease, often presenting with hematemesis or melena.
(Choice B)
Gastric outlet obstruction
Gastric outlet obstruction results from chronic inflammation and scarring, typically from duodenal ulcers near the pylorus. While significant when it occurs, it affects fewer than 5% of peptic ulcer patients compared to the 15-20% who experience bleeding.
(Choice C)
Penetration into adjacent structures
Penetration occurs when an ulcer erodes through the full thickness of the gastric or duodenal wall into an adjacent organ (pancreas, liver, omentum) but remains contained. This complication is much less frequent than hemorrhage.
(Choice D)
Ulcer perforation
Ulcer perforation is a serious but less common complication of peptic ulcer disease, occurring in approximately 2-10% of cases compared to bleeding which occurs in 15-20% of cases.
(Choice E)
Development of chronic atrophic gastritis
Chronic atrophic gastritis is associated with H. pylori infection and peptic ulcer disease but represents an inflammatory process rather than an acute complication requiring immediate intervention like hemorrhage.

pages.question:
A 32-year-old woman reports struggling with low energy, feelings of sadness, and irregular menstrual cycles for the last three months. She recently started noticing milk discharge from her breasts. She uses oral contraceptive pills. Her medical history is unremarkable, and she is not on any medication. Physical examination reveals dry skin, sparse eyebrows, and a goiter. Her gynecological exam is normal. Laboratory findings show: 

Serum pregnancy test Negative 
Free T4 2.8	μg/dL
Serum TSH 9.8
Prolactin 32 ng/mL 
Antithyroid peroxidase antibodies Positive 

What is the likely mechanism behind the association of hypothyroidism with hyperprolactinemia in this patient?

answers.text:
Antithyroid peroxidase antibodies stimulate dopamine production
(3.36%)

Antithyroid peroxidase antibodies inhibit dopamine production
(2.52%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
In primary hypothyroidism, decreased thyroid hormone levels lead to increased TRH secretion from the hypothalamus. TRH not only stimulates TSH release but also directly stimulates prolactin secretion from anterior pituitary lactotrophs, resulting in hyperprolactinemia. This elevated prolactin can cause galactorrhea and menstrual irregularities, as seen in this patient with Hashimoto's thyroiditis.
(Choice A)
TSH stimulates dopamine production
Incorrect. TSH has no role in dopamine production or regulation. TSH functions specifically to stimulate thyroid hormone synthesis and release from the thyroid gland. The mechanism of hyperprolactinemia in hypothyroidism involves TRH directly stimulating prolactin secretion from anterior pituitary lactotrophs.
(Choice B)
TRH stimulates prolactin production
Correct because increased TRH levels in hypothyroidism can result in elevated prolactin production, contributing to hyperprolactinemia.
(Choice C)
Antithyroid peroxidase antibodies stimulate dopamine production
Incorrect. Antithyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) antibodies are markers of autoimmune thyroid disease and contribute to thyroid destruction, but they have no direct effect on dopamine production or the hypothalamic-pituitary dopamine pathways that regulate prolactin.
(Choice D)
Antithyroid peroxidase antibodies inhibit dopamine production
Incorrect. Anti-TPO antibodies are involved in autoimmune destruction of thyroid tissue in Hashimoto's thyroiditis but do not affect dopamine production or secretion. The hyperprolactinemia in this patient results from elevated TRH levels directly stimulating prolactin release, not from antibody effects on dopamine pathways.
(Choice E)
TSH inhibits dopamine production
Incorrect. TSH does not interfere with dopamine production or secretion. TSH acts primarily on thyroid follicular cells to stimulate thyroid hormone synthesis. The hyperprolactinemia seen in hypothyroidism results from elevated TRH levels directly stimulating prolactin release, not from TSH effects on dopamine.

pages.question:
A 28-week gestational age male infant is delivered via emergency cesarean section due to placental abruption. The infant is limp at birth with Apgar scores of 3 and 7 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. He develops tachypnea, grunting, and cyanosis requiring endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation. Arterial blood gas on 60% FiO2 is shown below. Increasing FiO2 to 100% improves PaO2 to only 60 mm Hg. Chest x-ray reveals a hazy ground-glass appearance with reduced lung volumes. Which of the following best explains the persistent hypoxemia despite high inspired oxygen concentration?



pH	7.26
PaCO2	58 mm Hg
PaO2	68 mm Hg
HCO3	25 mEq/L
Base excess	-4 mEq/L
SaO2	92 %
Lactate	2.0 mmol/L

answers.text:
Left-to-right shunting through patent ductus arteriosus
(6.32%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
Preterm neonate with clinical and radiographic features of respiratory distress syndrome demonstrating persistent hypoxia despite 100% oxygen supplementation, indicative of intrapulmonary right-to-left shunting due to ventilation/perfusion mismatch.
(Choice A)
Increased intrapulmonary right-to-left shunting
In neonatal RDS, surfactant deficiency causes alveolar collapse (atelectasis), leading to ventilation/perfusion mismatch where blood flows through non-ventilated lung regions, resulting in intrapulmonary shunting and hypoxia that does not fully respond to increased FiO2.
(Choice B)
Hypoventilation
Hypoventilation causes both hypercapnia and hypoxia, but hypoxia from hypoventilation typically improves dramatically with supplemental oxygen. The persistent hypoxia despite 100% FiO2 indicates intrapulmonary shunting, not hypoventilation.
(Choice C)
Diffusion impairment
While diffusion impairment can contribute to hypoxia in some lung diseases, in neonatal RDS the primary mechanism causing hypoxia that is unresponsive to supplemental oxygen is intrapulmonary shunting. Blood flows through collapsed, non-ventilated alveoli, bypassing gas exchange entirely, which cannot be corrected by increasing FiO2.
(Choice D)
Left-to-right shunting through patent ductus arteriosus
A patent ductus arteriosus with left-to-right shunting increases pulmonary blood flow and can cause congestive heart failure, but it does not cause significant arterial hypoxia. The refractory hypoxia seen here (poor response to 100% FiO2) is characteristic of intrapulmonary shunting from RDS, not cardiac shunting.
(Choice E)
Reduced cardiac output
While reduced cardiac output can cause tissue hypoxia and poor oxygen delivery, it would not prevent PaO2 from improving with high FiO2. The lack of improvement in arterial PaO2 despite 100% oxygen indicates intrapulmonary shunting where blood bypasses ventilated alveoli.

pages.question: A 32-year-old man with no significant past medical history presents with a 3-day history of progressive bilateral leg weakness and urinary incontinence. He reports a prior episode 18 months ago of transient diplopia and vertigo that resolved spontaneously after 2 weeks. Neurological examination reveals spastic paraparesis, hyperreflexia in the lower extremities, and a sensory level at T10. MRI of the brain and spine shows multiple hyperintense lesions in the periventricular white matter and spinal cord on T2-weighted imaging, consistent with demyelination. Lumbar puncture is performed. Which of the following is the most likely cerebrospinal fluid finding in this patient?

answers.text:
Oligoclonal bands with normal cell count
(92.45%)

Granulomatous inflammation with angiotensin-converting enzyme elevation
(0%)

Opening pressure of >250 mmH2O with normal cell count and protein
(1.89%)

Neutrophilic pleocytosis of >1000 cells/μL with glucose of <40 mg/dL
(0%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient's symptoms of relapsing-remitting neurologic deficits (prior diplopia and vertigo, current spastic paraparesis and sensory loss) disseminated in space and time, combined with characteristic MRI findings, suggest multiple sclerosis (MS). Cerebrospinal fluid analysis in MS typically reveals oligoclonal bands in 85%-95% of patients, indicating intrathecal immunoglobulin synthesis, with normal opening pressure, cell count, and protein levels. The other choices represent CSF patterns seen in idiopathic intracranial hypertension (elevated pressure), viral meningitis (lymphocytic pleocytosis), Guillain-Barré syndrome (albuminocytologic dissociation), subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (measles antibodies), bacterial meningitis (neutrophilic pleocytosis with low glucose), and neurosarcoidosis (granulomatous inflammation with elevated ACE).
(Choice A)
Oligoclonal bands with normal cell count
This is the characteristic CSF finding in MS, indicating intrathecal immunoglobulin production.
(Choice B)
Granulomatous inflammation with angiotensin-converting enzyme elevation
Granulomatous inflammation with elevated ACE levels suggests neurosarcoidosis. While neurosarcoidosis can mimic MS with CNS lesions, it typically shows enhancement patterns and cranial nerve involvement not seen in this case.
(Choice C)
Opening pressure of >250 mmH2O with normal cell count and protein
Elevated opening pressure with normal cell count is characteristic of idiopathic intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri). MS typically has normal opening pressure (100-180 mmH2O).
(Choice D)
Neutrophilic pleocytosis of >1000 cells/μL with glucose of <40 mg/dL
This indicates bacterial meningitis, which presents acutely with fever and meningismus, unlike MS.
(Choice E)
Lymphocytic pleocytosis with elevated protein
Lymphocytic pleocytosis with elevated protein suggests viral CNS infection or post-infectious demyelination (ADEM). MS characteristically has normal or only mildly elevated cell counts (<50 cells/μL).

pages.question: A 28-year-old woman presents to the ophthalmology clinic with sudden onset of blurred vision and double vision in her right eye that began after a minor fall while hiking. She denies any direct eye trauma but reports occasional joint dislocations and a family history of sudden cardiac deaths in young relatives. On physical examination, she is tall and slender with arachnodactyly and a high-arched palate. Slit-lamp examination reveals iridodonesis (tremulous iris) and anterior displacement of the lens in the right eye. Visual acuity is decreased in the affected eye, but fundus examination is normal. In addition to referral for potential surgical lens correction, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in this patient's management?

answers.text:
Brain MRI to evaluate for intracranial vascular malformations
(1.43%)

Genetic testing for fibrillin-1 gene mutation
(30%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient has ectopia lentis likely due to an underlying connective tissue disorder such as Marfan syndrome, given her physical features and family history. Ectopia lentis can cause acute vision changes with iris vibration and lens displacement, often triggered by minor trauma or occurring spontaneously in genetic conditions. Management includes refractive correction or surgery for the lens, but assessment for systemic complications, particularly aortic involvement, is crucial via echocardiography.
(Choice A)
Echocardiography
This is the correct next step to assess for aortic root dilation or aneurysm, a potentially life-threatening complication in Marfan syndrome, which is suggested by the patient's ectopia lentis, physical features, and family history.
(Choice B)
Brain MRI to evaluate for intracranial vascular malformations
Brain MRI is not indicated as the immediate next step. While patients with Marfan syndrome can have intracranial vascular abnormalities, there are no neurologic symptoms present, and cardiovascular assessment takes priority due to the higher immediate risk of aortic complications.
(Choice C)
Chest X-ray
Chest X-ray may show skeletal abnormalities but is insensitive for detecting aortic pathology compared to echocardiography in this context.
(Choice D)
Genetic testing for fibrillin-1 gene mutation
While genetic testing for fibrillin-1 mutations would confirm Marfan syndrome diagnosis, it is not the immediate priority. Urgent cardiovascular assessment with echocardiography takes precedence due to the potentially life-threatening risk of aortic root dilation and dissection.
(Choice E)
Electrocardiogram
While an ECG might detect cardiac conduction abnormalities or arrhythmias associated with Marfan syndrome, it cannot assess for aortic root dilation or aneurysm, which are the most serious and immediate cardiovascular concerns requiring echocardiographic evaluation.

pages.question: A 58-year-old woman with hypothyroidism and osteoporosis presents for a routine follow-up. She has been on levothyroxine 125 mcg daily for 5 years and was recently started on alendronate 70 mg weekly for osteoporosis prevention. She also takes a calcium carbonate supplement 1200 mg daily, which she began taking at the same time each morning as her other medications. Repeat TSH drawn 8 weeks after starting the new regimen is 9.8 mIU/L (previously 1.2 mIU/L). She denies missing doses. Her current medication schedule has her taking levothyroxine, alendronate, and calcium carbonate simultaneously at 7 AM with a glass of water. Which of the following best explains her elevated TSH and is the most appropriate next step in management?

answers.text:
Increase the levothyroxine dose to 150 mcg daily and continue taking all medications together at 7 AM
(0%)

Instruct the patient to take levothyroxine and alendronate first thing in the morning on an empty stomach and separate calcium carbonate by at least 4 hours
(100%)

Switch from calcium carbonate to calcium citrate and continue taking all medications together at the same time
(0%)

Order thyroid ultrasonography to evaluate for a new thyroid nodule causing suppressed hormone production
(0%)

Discontinue calcium supplementation permanently, as calcium cannot be safely used with levothyroxine
(0%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
Calcium carbonate significantly impairs the gastrointestinal absorption of both levothyroxine and bisphosphonates when taken simultaneously. Levothyroxine should be taken on an empty stomach 30-60 minutes before any calcium or other divalent cation supplements, and bisphosphonates must similarly be taken with plain water alone and patients should remain upright for 30 minutes. Separating these medications by at least 4 hours from calcium supplementation will restore adequate drug absorption and normalize thyroid function.
(Choice A)
Increase the levothyroxine dose to 150 mcg daily and continue taking all medications together at 7 AM
Simply increasing the levothyroxine dose without addressing the underlying absorption problem will not reliably correct the issue. Calcium carbonate chelates levothyroxine in the GI tract and prevents adequate absorption regardless of dose; the fundamental problem is the timing of co-administration, not the dose itself. Dose escalation without correcting the schedule risks over-replacement once the interaction is addressed.
(Choice B)
Instruct the patient to take levothyroxine and alendronate first thing in the morning on an empty stomach and separate calcium carbonate by at least 4 hours
Calcium carbonate forms insoluble complexes with levothyroxine in the GI tract, dramatically reducing its bioavailability and causing apparent hypothyroidism despite adequate dosing — a well-documented drug-supplement interaction. Levothyroxine must be taken on an empty stomach 30-60 minutes before food, coffee, or supplements to maximize absorption. Alendronate similarly requires administration with plain water alone on an empty stomach, and the patient must remain upright for 30 minutes afterward to prevent esophageal injury and ensure absorption. Calcium and other divalent cations (iron, magnesium) should be separated from both levothyroxine and bisphosphonates by at least 4 hours. Correcting the administration schedule — rather than changing doses — is the appropriate first step when this interaction is identified. After adjusting the schedule, TSH should be rechecked in 6-8 weeks to confirm normalization.
(Choice C)
Switch from calcium carbonate to calcium citrate and continue taking all medications together at the same time
Both calcium carbonate and calcium citrate interact with levothyroxine and can reduce its absorption when taken simultaneously. The interaction is a class effect of calcium supplementation on levothyroxine bioavailability, not specific to the carbonate salt form. Switching calcium formulations without addressing timing of administration will not reliably correct the elevated TSH.
(Choice D)
Order thyroid ultrasonography to evaluate for a new thyroid nodule causing suppressed hormone production
The clinical scenario provides a clear pharmacokinetic explanation for the elevated TSH — simultaneous ingestion of calcium with levothyroxine — making a structural thyroid etiology highly unlikely. The patient has established hypothyroidism that was previously well-controlled on the same levothyroxine dose, and the TSH elevation coincided with starting calcium supplementation. Thyroid ultrasound evaluates for nodules or structural disease but would not explain this sudden change in a previously stable patient. The timing correlation with supplement initiation makes drug-supplement interaction the most likely explanation, and addressing this interaction is the appropriate first step before pursuing unnecessary imaging studies.
(Choice E)
Discontinue calcium supplementation permanently, as calcium cannot be safely used with levothyroxine
Calcium supplementation is not contraindicated with levothyroxine; the interaction is a pharmacokinetic one related to timing of co-administration, not an absolute contraindication. Calcium is an important supplement for osteoporosis prevention in this patient and should not be discontinued. Simply separating the doses by 4 or more hours resolves the interaction and allows both medications to be used safely.

pages.question: A 32-year-old man with a history of panic disorder presents to the emergency department with complaints of severe restlessness, irritability, hand tremors, insomnia, and vivid nightmares that began 36 hours ago. He reports that he has been taking alprazolam 1 mg three times daily for the past 4 months as prescribed by his psychiatrist. Three days ago, he ran out of his medication while on a business trip and was unable to refill it immediately. He denies any recent alcohol use, illicit drug intake, or changes in his other medications, which include sertraline for his anxiety. Vital signs show tachycardia and elevated blood pressure, but physical examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient's sudden onset of restlessness, irritability, tremors, insomnia, and nightmares 36 hours after abruptly stopping alprazolam are classic for benzodiazepine withdrawal syndrome. Short-acting benzodiazepines like alprazolam have withdrawal symptoms that typically emerge within 1-3 days of cessation and can include rebound anxiety that may be more severe than the original condition. The continued use of sertraline makes antidepressant discontinuation syndrome unlikely, and the acute temporal relationship to benzodiazepine cessation distinguishes this from medical conditions like hyperthyroidism.
(Choice A)
Hyperthyroidism
Hyperthyroidism can cause anxiety, tremors, and tachycardia but typically presents with additional signs such as weight loss, heat intolerance, palpitations, or thyromegaly. The acute onset temporally related to benzodiazepine cessation makes withdrawal more likely.
(Choice B)
Exacerbation of underlying panic disorder
While symptoms may resemble a panic attack, the temporal association with medication discontinuation and the presence of tremors and insomnia suggest withdrawal rather than a simple recurrence of the underlying condition.
(Choice C)
Caffeine intoxication
Caffeine intoxication typically requires consumption of >250mg caffeine and causes jitteriness, insomnia, and mild tremors, but rarely causes the severe autonomic symptoms or vivid nightmares seen in this patient. The temporal relationship to alprazolam cessation is more suggestive of benzodiazepine withdrawal.
(Choice D)
Benzodiazepine withdrawal
The acute onset of symptoms matching benzodiazepine withdrawal syndrome after abrupt cessation of alprazolam, a short-acting benzodiazepine, supports this diagnosis. Early symptoms include rebound anxiety, insomnia, and autonomic hyperactivity.
(Choice E)
Sertraline withdrawal
Sertraline discontinuation syndrome typically requires abrupt cessation after weeks to months of use and presents with flu-like symptoms, dizziness, and 'brain zaps' rather than the autonomic hyperactivity and tremors seen here. The patient's sertraline was continued, making this unlikely.

pages.question: A 42-year-old man with a history of liver transplantation 6 months ago and ongoing immunosuppressive therapy presents with numerous pruritic, skin-colored papules scattered across his trunk, arms, and genitals as shown below. Despite initial treatment with curettage, new lesions continue to develop, and the condition has persisted for over 4 months. The patient reports no recent sexual activity or exposure to children with similar rashes. What is the most likely underlying factor contributing to the widespread and prolonged course of this dermatologic condition?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient's presentation is consistent with molluscum contagiosum, a poxvirus infection characterized by smooth, dome-shaped, umbilicated papules. In immunocompetent individuals, molluscum contagiosum is typically self-limited and resolves within 6-24 months. However, in patients with impaired T-cell mediated immunity (such as from post-transplant immunosuppressive therapy), the infection becomes more extensive, persistent, and treatment-resistant. The cellular immune system, particularly CD4+ and CD8+ T-cells, is crucial for viral clearance. Management includes physical destruction (curettage, cryotherapy, laser), topical immunomodulators (imiquimod), or topical retinoids, though resolution may be significantly delayed in immunocompromised patients.
(Choice A)
Humoral immunodeficiency
Humoral immunodeficiency primarily affects B-cell function and antibody production, leading to recurrent sinopulmonary bacterial infections rather than prolonged viral skin infections like molluscum contagiosum. While some immunoglobulin deficiencies can have associated T-cell abnormalities, the primary defect does not explain this presentation.
(Choice B)
Classical complement pathway deficiency
Complement deficiencies predispose to encapsulated bacterial infections and some autoimmune conditions, but they do not typically cause extensive or persistent molluscum contagiosum.
(Choice C)
Cellular immunodeficiency
Impaired cellular immunity, such as from immunosuppressive therapy post-transplant, leads to widespread and persistent molluscum contagiosum due to reduced T-cell mediated clearance of the poxvirus.
(Choice D)
Primary neutrophil dysfunction
Neutrophil dysfunction disorders (such as chronic granulomatous disease or neutrophil adhesion defects) predispose patients to recurrent bacterial and fungal infections, particularly with catalase-positive organisms. These disorders do not significantly impair the cellular immune response needed to clear viral infections like molluscum contagiosum.
(Choice E)
Eosinophil hyperactivity
Eosinophil hyperactivity or eosinophilia is typically associated with allergic conditions, parasitic infections, or certain malignancies. Eosinophils do not play a significant role in antiviral immunity against poxviruses like molluscum contagiosum, making this an unlikely contributing factor to the persistent infection.

pages.question: A 45-year-old Latino male arrives at the clinic due to a painless lump noticed on his neck during a shower. He denies any recent illnesses, voice changes, or swallowing difficulties, and mentions stable weight and regular bowel movements. His mother had thyroid issues when she was in her 50s. His vitals include a blood pressure of 125/85 mm Hg, heart rate of 72/min, a respiratory rate of 18/min, and a temperature of 36.6°C (97.9°F). On examination, you observe a solitary, firm, mobile 1.5 x 1 cm nodule on the right side of the thyroid. There is no lymphadenopathy. The clinical examination yields no additional findings. What is the most appropriate initial diagnostic step?

answers.text:
Conducting a Biopsy with Fine Needle Aspiration
(1.24%)

Obtaining a CT Scan of the Neck
(0%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
Thyroid nodules are common and require systematic evaluation. The initial step is always serum TSH measurement to assess thyroid function. If TSH is normal or elevated, ultrasound follows to evaluate nodule characteristics and guide biopsy decisions based on suspicious features. If TSH is suppressed, radionuclide scanning helps identify hyperfunctioning ('hot') nodules, which are rarely malignant. This TSH-first approach ensures appropriate risk stratification and cost-effective management.
(Choice A)
Conducting a Biopsy with Fine Needle Aspiration
Fine needle aspiration biopsy is indicated based on nodule characteristics found on ultrasound and thyroid function status. TSH must be checked first to determine if the nodule is hyperfunctioning (which rarely requires biopsy) before proceeding to tissue sampling.
(Choice B)
Performing Ultrasound Imaging
While thyroid ultrasound is valuable for characterizing nodule features and guiding biopsy decisions, TSH measurement takes precedence as the initial step to determine thyroid functional status, which influences the entire diagnostic algorithm.
(Choice C)
Administering a Radionuclide Thyroid Scan
Reserved for cases where TSH is low, indicating potential hyperfunctioning nodules (hot nodules).
(Choice D)
Checking Serum TSH Levels
Evaluating serum TSH is essential for determining the functional status of the thyroid gland and guiding further diagnostic work-up.
(Choice E)
Obtaining a CT Scan of the Neck
CT scans offer anatomical details but are unnecessary as a primary step in thyroid nodule evaluation.

pages.question:
A 48-year-old woman presents to the clinic with progressive shortness of breath on exertion, orthopnea, and lower extremity edema over the past 6 months. She has a history of poorly controlled hypertension, obstructive sleep apnea treated with CPAP, and frequent headaches. She reports that her rings no longer fit her fingers and her shoe size has increased from 7 to 9 over the last few years. Physical examination reveals prognathism, macroglossia, widely spaced teeth, and enlarged hands and feet. Laboratory values are shown below. An echocardiogram is performed to evaluate her cardiac function. Which of the following is the most likely finding on echocardiography?



WBC Count	7200 /µL
Neutrophils	60 %
Lymphocytes	30 %
Hemoglobin	13.5 g/dL
Hematocrit	40 %
RBC Count	4.6 million/µL
Platelet Count	250000 /µL
IGF-1	450 ng/mL (range: 100–300 ng/mL)
Sodium	140 mEq/L
Potassium	4.2 mEq/L
Chloride	103 mEq/L
Bicarbonate (HCO3-)	24 mEq/L
Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN)	15 mg/dL
Creatinine	0.9 mg/dL
Glucose	92 mg/dL
Calcium	9.2 mg/dL
Phosphate	3.5 mg/dL
Magnesium	2.0 mg/dL
AST (SGOT)	28 U/L
ALT (SGPT)	32 U/L

answers.text:
Eccentric left ventricular hypertrophy with dilation
(30.77%)

Global hypokinesis with reduced ejection fraction
(15.38%)

Normal left ventricular wall thickness and function
(2.2%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient has clinical features suggestive of acromegaly, including prognathism, macroglossia, enlarged extremities, and elevated IGF-1. Growth hormone excess in acromegaly causes concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, initially leading to diastolic dysfunction with preserved systolic function. As the disease progresses, systolic dysfunction may develop. Concurrent hypertension and obstructive sleep apnea further exacerbate the cardiomyopathy. The most likely echocardiographic finding in this stage of disease is concentric left ventricular hypertrophy.
(Choice A)
Eccentric left ventricular hypertrophy with dilation
Eccentric left ventricular hypertrophy with chamber dilation is characteristic of volume overload states (like mitral or aortic regurgitation) rather than the pressure overload pattern seen in acromegaly. Growth hormone excess typically causes concentric hypertrophy with wall thickening but preserved chamber dimensions in early stages.
(Choice B)
Global hypokinesis with reduced ejection fraction
Global hypokinesis with reduced ejection fraction represents advanced acromegaly cardiomyopathy with systolic dysfunction. However, this patient's presentation suggests earlier-stage disease where concentric hypertrophy with preserved systolic function (but impaired diastolic function) is the predominant finding.
(Choice C)
Normal left ventricular wall thickness and function
Given the patient's symptoms and acromegaly features, normal findings would be unlikely; hypertrophy is a common cardiac complication.
(Choice D)
Concentric left ventricular hypertrophy
This is the correct finding. Acromegaly leads to growth hormone-induced concentric hypertrophy of the myocardium, initially causing diastolic dysfunction.
(Choice E)
Isolated aortic valve stenosis
While acromegaly can be associated with valvular disease, the primary cardiac manifestation is myocardial hypertrophy rather than isolated valvular stenosis.

pages.question: A 58-year-old woman with a 30-pack-year smoking history and type 2 diabetes mellitus presents to her primary care physician complaining of cramping pain in her buttocks and thighs that develops predictably after climbing stairs or walking uphill for about 5 minutes. The pain resolves completely within 2-3 minutes of rest. She denies pain at rest or skin changes in her legs. Physical examination reveals diminished femoral pulses bilaterally, but normal popliteal and pedal pulses. Ankle-brachial index is 0.65 on the right and 0.68 on the left. Duplex ultrasonography shows stenosis in the aortoiliac arteries. In addition to smoking cessation counseling and optimization of her diabetes and lipid management, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

answers.text:
Advise bed rest and leg elevation
(0%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
The patient's symptoms are consistent with intermittent claudication due to aortoiliac peripheral artery disease. Initial treatment should include a supervised exercise program along with aggressive risk factor modification. Pharmacologic agents like cilostazol and revascularization procedures are reserved for patients with persistent limiting symptoms despite conservative management.
(Choice A)
Recommend a supervised exercise program
Supervised exercise therapy is the cornerstone of initial management for intermittent claudication in peripheral artery disease, improving walking distance and quality of life.
(Choice B)
Refer for percutaneous transluminal angioplasty
Percutaneous transluminal angioplasty is reserved for patients with severe, lifestyle-limiting claudication that persists despite at least 3-6 months of optimal medical therapy including supervised exercise. Initial management should always begin with conservative measures including exercise therapy and risk factor modification.
(Choice C)
Prescribe pentoxifylline
Pentoxifylline, a hemorrheologic agent, has shown minimal clinical benefit in randomized trials and is not recommended in current guidelines for peripheral artery disease. Supervised exercise therapy has superior evidence for improving functional capacity and quality of life in claudication.
(Choice D)
Advise bed rest and leg elevation
Bed rest and leg elevation are counterproductive in peripheral artery disease with claudication. These measures do not improve arterial blood flow and lead to deconditioning, which worsens functional capacity. Active exercise therapy promotes collateral circulation development and improves symptoms.
(Choice E)
Initiate cilostazol therapy
Cilostazol is a phosphodiesterase inhibitor that can improve walking distance in claudication, but current guidelines recommend supervised exercise therapy as first-line treatment. Cilostazol should be considered only after a trial of supervised exercise and when symptoms remain lifestyle-limiting despite optimal medical therapy.

pages.question: A 4-month-old infant of Italian descent is brought to the pediatric clinic due to episodic hypoglycemic episodes and irritability. He has a characteristic round, cherubic face with full cheeks, a lean build with noticeable thin limbs, and a distended abdomen. On examination, the liver edge is palpable 4 cm below the right costal margin and the kidneys appear enlarged on ultrasound. Laboratory tests show a blood glucose level of 45 mg/dL, with elevated lactic acid, uric acid, cholesterol, and triglycerides. Liver enzymes are within normal limits. What is the likely underlying diagnosis?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
Von Gierke's disease (type I glycogen storage disease) is the most probable diagnosis given the combination of severe fasting hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, hyperlipidemia, and characteristic phenotype with normal liver transaminases. The key distinguishing feature from other glycogen storage diseases is the specific metabolic profile of elevated lactate and uric acid with normal liver enzymes, unlike type III which shows elevated transaminases.
(Choice A)
Glycogen debranching enzyme deficiency
Cori disease (type III glycogen storage disease) presents with hepatomegaly and hypoglycemia similar to type I, but is distinguished by elevated liver transaminases, ketosis during fasting, and normal or only mildly elevated lactate levels. This patient's normal liver enzymes and elevated lactate make type I more likely.
(Choice B)
Glycogen branching enzyme deficiency
Andersen disease (type IV glycogen storage disease) is caused by glycogen branching enzyme deficiency and leads to progressive hepatic fibrosis and cirrhosis. Patients typically present with failure to thrive and progressive liver dysfunction rather than the acute metabolic derangements (hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis) seen in this case.
(Choice C)
Liver phosphorylase deficiency
Hers disease (type VI glycogen storage disease) is caused by liver phosphorylase deficiency and typically presents with mild hepatomegaly and growth retardation. Unlike type I disease, patients do not develop lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, or the severe metabolic derangements seen in this case.
(Choice D)
Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency
Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency, or Von Gierke's disease (type I glycogen storage disease), is characterized by persistent hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, and hyperlipidemia. The phenotype includes delicate limbs, doll-like facial features, and organomegaly without elevated transaminases.
(Choice E)
Lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency
Pompe disease (type II glycogen storage disease) is caused by lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency and primarily presents with progressive muscle weakness and cardiomyopathy. The infantile form presents in the first months of life with severe cardiomyopathy and hypotonia, not the metabolic derangements (lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia) seen in this case.

pages.question: A 18-year-old Caucasian male is brought to the emergency department by his roommate due to recent erratic behavior. Normally jovial and responsible, he has become noticeably more aggressive and erratic over the past ten days. He made substantial withdrawals from his savings account to host frequent parties, insisting they are attended by 'foreign dignitaries.' When asked, he claims to be an undercover agent for a foreign agency monitoring local activities. On examination, vital signs are temperature 37.0°C (98.6°F), blood pressure 140/90 mm Hg, pulse 110/min, and respirations 20/min. His pupils are noticeably dilated, and he appears restless but cooperative. What's the most likely diagnosis?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient’s clinical presentation, featuring sudden erratic behavior with physiological signs like dilated pupils, tachycardia, and hypertension, fits the profile for amphetamine intoxication. Amphetamines enhance catecholamine release in the brain, producing stimulant effects. Such intake can also cause delusions and hallucinations due to overstimulation of the CNS, distinguishing it from other related disorders and intoxicants.
(Choice A)
Amphetamine intoxication
The acute onset of erratic behavior, delusions, tachycardia, hypertension, and mydriasis are characteristic of amphetamine intoxication. These stimulants can trigger psychotic symptoms like those presented.
(Choice B)
Bipolar I disorder, manic episode
While manic episodes can present with grandiose delusions, decreased need for sleep, and increased goal-directed activity, the acute 10-day timeline with prominent physiological signs (dilated pupils, tachycardia, hypertension) strongly suggests substance intoxication rather than a primary mood disorder. Mania typically has a more gradual onset.
(Choice C)
Hallucinogen intoxication
LSD intoxication typically causes more perceptual distortions, visual hallucinations, and disorganized thinking rather than the organized grandiose delusions seen here. While LSD can cause mydriasis, it rarely causes the hypertension and tachycardia prominent in this case.
(Choice D)
Acute stress disorder
Acute stress disorder requires exposure to a traumatic event and occurs within one month of the trauma. This patient has no reported trauma exposure. Additionally, the combination of dilated pupils, tachycardia, and hypertension suggests substance intoxication rather than a stress-related disorder.
(Choice E)
Schizophreniform disorder
To be diagnosed with schizophreniform disorder, symptoms similar to schizophrenia must persist for at least one month. This patient's symptoms have only been present for ten days.

pages.question: A 7-year-old girl is brought to the clinic by her father for loud snoring and restless sleep. Her father reports she wakes up frequently at night, occasionally gasps during sleep, and has been struggling to concentrate in school. Her teacher has noted behavioral difficulties and inattention. Her weight is 42 kg and height is 118 cm (BMI 30.2 kg/m², above the 99th percentile for age and sex). Vital signs are normal. Physical exam reveals mild tonsillar enlargement (2+), a crowded oropharynx, and mild nasal congestion. Neck circumference is increased. Which of the following obesity-related comorbidity should be highest on the differential diagnosis and warrants urgent evaluation?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
Pediatric obesity significantly increases the risk of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) due to upper airway soft tissue enlargement and reduced pharyngeal muscle tone. OSA presents with snoring, witnessed apneas, restless sleep, and neurobehavioral consequences including inattention and behavioral problems that frequently mimic ADHD. Overnight polysomnography is the gold standard diagnostic test. Early recognition and treatment of OSA in obese children is essential, as untreated OSA contributes to cardiovascular complications, metabolic dysfunction, poor academic performance, and behavioral problems.
(Choice A)
Type 2 diabetes mellitus
Type 2 diabetes is an important obesity-related comorbidity to screen for in children with obesity using fasting glucose or HbA1c, especially in those with acanthosis nigricans or a family history of diabetes. However, the presenting symptoms in this vignette — snoring, gasping, restless sleep, and neurobehavioral problems — are not attributable to diabetes and are most consistent with obstructive sleep apnea. Diabetes screening can be performed as part of routine metabolic evaluation but does not represent the most urgent concern here.
(Choice B)
Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease
NAFLD is an important obesity-related comorbidity that should be screened for with liver function tests (ALT, AST) in children with obesity, but it typically presents asymptomatically and does not explain the sleep-related symptoms, nocturnal gasping, and neurobehavioral findings described in this vignette. The clinical presentation is dominated by sleep-disordered breathing symptoms, making OSA the most urgent diagnosis requiring immediate evaluation with polysomnography. NAFLD screening remains appropriate as part of comprehensive metabolic evaluation.
(Choice C)
Obstructive sleep apnea
Obstructive sleep apnea is the highest-priority obesity-related comorbidity in this clinical scenario. Pediatric obesity significantly increases the risk of OSA due to fat deposition in the pharyngeal soft tissues, increased neck circumference, and reduced upper airway tone during sleep. Classic features — loud snoring, witnessed gasping, restless sleep, and nighttime awakenings — are all present in this child. Neurobehavioral consequences of OSA in children, including inattention, behavioral difficulties, and academic underperformance, are well established and are frequently mistaken for primary ADHD. Overnight polysomnography (sleep study) is the gold standard diagnostic tool for pediatric OSA. Untreated OSA in children is associated with cardiovascular complications including systemic hypertension, left ventricular hypertrophy, and metabolic dysfunction. Management typically involves adenotonsillectomy as first-line therapy in children with tonsillar hypertrophy, along with obesity management to address the underlying risk factor.
(Choice D)
Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder
While inattention and behavioral problems are present, these symptoms in a child with obesity, loud snoring, gasping, and restless sleep are most consistent with sleep-disordered breathing causing secondary neurobehavioral consequences, not primary ADHD. OSA is well-documented to cause inattention, hyperactivity, and behavioral dysregulation in children that can mimic ADHD. Treating the underlying OSA often resolves these symptoms without need for stimulant medication. Current guidelines recommend ruling out sleep disorders before diagnosing ADHD in children with sleep-related symptoms.
(Choice E)
Hypothyroidism
Hypothyroidism can contribute to weight gain and fatigue in children and should be considered in the evaluation of obesity, but it is less likely to cause the discrete nighttime gasping and witnessed apneas described in this vignette. While TSH measurement is reasonable as part of an obesity workup, the constellation of snoring, apneas, restless sleep, and behavioral consequences is classic for obstructive sleep apnea in an obese child and warrants polysomnography as the priority evaluation.

pages.question:
A 50-year-old diabetic woman is admitted to the hospital after being found disoriented in her apartment. Her vital signs indicate a temperature of 37.8°C (100.1°F), heart rate of 115 bpm, blood pressure of 88/60 mmHg, and respirations of 20/min. Blood samples are taken, and initial laboratory results show: 

Sodium: 132 mEq/L
Potassium: 4.5 mEq/L
Chloride: 98 mEq/L
Bicarbonate: 20 mEq/L
Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN): 21 mg/dl
Glucose: 960 mg/dL
Calcium: 9.8 mg/dL

Amylase: 90 U/L
AST: 18 U/L
ALT: 22 U/L
Ammonia: 10 micro-mol/L (Normal: 9-33)

PT: 12.5 seconds
APTT: 28 seconds

Arterial blood gases:
PH: 7.36
PaCO2: 40 mmHg
PaO2: 88 mmHg

What is the most appropriate initial therapy for this patient?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS) presents with severe hyperglycemia, hyperosmolality, and profound dehydration leading to hemodynamic instability. The cornerstone of initial management is aggressive fluid resuscitation with isotonic saline to restore intravascular volume, improve tissue perfusion, and stabilize blood pressure. Fluid replacement also helps lower glucose levels through dilution and improved renal glucose clearance, setting the stage for safe insulin administration once hemodynamic stability is achieved.
(Choice A)
Half normal saline
Half normal saline is typically used later in HHS management once hemodynamic stability is achieved and serum osmolality begins to decline. Using hypotonic saline initially in a hemodynamically unstable patient could worsen hypotension and delay restoration of intravascular volume.
(Choice B)
Dextrose 5% in water
This is not recommended initially since glucose levels are critically high; it’s used once glucose level decreases significantly to prevent hypoglycemia.
(Choice C)
Isotonic saline
Immediate fluid resuscitation with isotonic saline is critical to stabilize blood pressure and improve circulation in hyperosmolar hyperglycemic states.
(Choice D)
Insulin infusion
While insulin therapy is essential in HHS management, fluid resuscitation must be prioritized in hemodynamically unstable patients. Starting insulin before adequate fluid replacement can worsen hypotension by causing rapid fluid shifts and further intravascular volume depletion.
(Choice E)
Intravenous potassium
The patient's potassium level is currently normal (4.5 mEq/L), but potassium replacement becomes necessary once insulin therapy begins, as insulin drives potassium intracellularly and can cause dangerous hypokalemia. Potassium should only be added after confirming adequate urine output to prevent hyperkalemia.

pages.question:
A 42-year-old woman with no significant past medical history is admitted to the intensive care unit after a motor vehicle accident resulting in multiple fractures, abdominal trauma, and hemorrhagic shock. She requires mechanical ventilation and vasopressor support for ongoing hypotension. On hospital day 3, her serum glucose level is found to be 38 mg/dL despite adequate nutritional support via total parenteral nutrition and no history of diabetes or use of glucose-lowering medications. Laboratory values are shown below. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism underlying this patient's hypoglycemia? 



White Blood Cell Count	7.8 x10^3/µL
Hemoglobin	13.5 g/dL
Hematocrit	40%
Platelet Count	250 x10^3/µL
C-Reactive Protein (CRP)	45 mg/L
Procalcitonin	5.2 ng/mL
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient has critical illness following polytrauma with hemorrhagic shock, leading to systemic inflammation and hypoglycemia without diabetes or antidiabetic medications, consistent with increased glucose utilization in tissues due to inflammatory cytokines and suppression of hepatic gluconeogenesis. Enhanced hepatic gluconeogenesis would prevent hypoglycemia, excessive insulin secretion is suppressed in critical illness, adrenal insufficiency typically presents with hyponatremia and hyperkalemia and does not resolve with fluids alone, glycogen depletion is more common in prolonged malnutrition, sympathetic activation causes hyperglycemia, and medication effects from vasopressors do not typically cause hypoglycemia.
(Choice A)
Sympathetic nervous system activation
Sympathetic activation in stress responses typically leads to hyperglycemia through glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, not hypoglycemia.
(Choice B)
Increased tissue glucose utilization
In critical illness, inflammatory cytokines promote increased glucose uptake and utilization in tissues while suppressing hepatic gluconeogenesis, leading to hypoglycemia.
(Choice C)
Excessive insulin secretion
Insulin secretion is often suppressed in sepsis and critical illness due to stress hormones and cytokines, leading to hyperglycemia rather than hypoglycemia.
(Choice D)
Glycogen depletion from prolonged fasting
Glycogen depletion from fasting could contribute to hypoglycemia, but this patient is receiving adequate nutritional support via total parenteral nutrition. Additionally, glycogen stores are typically depleted within 12-24 hours of fasting, and this mechanism alone would not explain hypoglycemia in a well-nourished patient receiving TPN.
(Choice E)
Adrenal insufficiency
While adrenal insufficiency can cause hypoglycemia due to cortisol deficiency, it typically presents with additional classic features such as hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and hypotension that is refractory to fluid resuscitation. This patient's presentation is more consistent with critical illness-induced hypoglycemia from inflammatory processes.

pages.question: A large urban hospital's intensive care unit (ICU) has recently reported multiple instances of medication errors and delays in responding to patient deteriorations, attributed to poor communication and collaboration among the multidisciplinary team, including physicians, nurses, respiratory therapists, and pharmacists. A root cause analysis reveals issues with hierarchical barriers and lack of shared understanding during high-stress situations. The ICU director wants to implement a strategy to enhance team collaboration and prevent future incidents. Which of the following interventions is most likely to achieve this goal?

answers.text:
Implementing electronic communication tools for all team members
(33.75%)

Having respiratory therapists co-lead structured debriefings after critical ICU events
(28.75%)

Mandating annual team-building retreats for all ICU staff members
(12.5%)

Assigning a dedicated team coordinator to oversee all ICU shifts
(16.25%)

Requiring all team members to complete standardized online modules on communication skills
(8.75%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
The ICU team's issues stem from poor interprofessional collaboration. Implementing structured debriefings after critical events, co-led by respiratory therapists, can improve collaboration by fostering psychological safety, reducing hierarchy, enhancing coordination, and promoting a shared understanding of team goals.
(Choice A)
Implementing electronic communication tools for all team members
Electronic communication tools can improve information sharing but do not address the core issues of hierarchical barriers or foster the psychological safety needed for effective interprofessional collaboration during high-stress situations.
(Choice B)
Having respiratory therapists co-lead structured debriefings after critical ICU events
Structured debriefings co-led by non-physician team members like respiratory therapists enhance interprofessional collaboration by reducing hierarchy, improving coordination, and fostering psychological safety.
(Choice C)
Mandating annual team-building retreats for all ICU staff members
While team-building retreats can foster relationships, they are not structured around specific clinical events and do not directly address real-time collaboration issues in the ICU setting.
(Choice D)
Assigning a dedicated team coordinator to oversee all ICU shifts
While a team coordinator can help with workflow organization, this approach does not address the underlying communication barriers or provide the structured interprofessional discussions needed to improve collaboration and shared understanding after critical events.
(Choice E)
Requiring all team members to complete standardized online modules on communication skills
Online communication modules provide theoretical knowledge but lack the interactive, real-time application needed to break down hierarchical barriers and improve team dynamics during actual critical events.

pages.question: A 27-year-old pregnant woman, currently 13 weeks along, reports to her healthcare provider complaining of a consistent vaginal discharge with an unpleasant odor. She mentions being sexually active but has no history of past similar issues. On examination, there is an absence of inflammation or swelling on the vaginal walls or vulva, though a greyish, malodorous discharge is observable. Cervical and adnexal areas are non-tender. A saline wet mount examination reveals epithelial cells with a bacterial coat, and there are no visible white blood cells. What is the most appropriate treatment option for this patient?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
The presence of clue cells on microscopic examination is diagnostic of bacterial vaginosis. Metronidazole is the first-line treatment as it effectively targets the polymicrobial infection, particularly Gardnerella vaginalis. Treatment during pregnancy is important to prevent complications such as preterm birth and low birth weight.
(Choice A)
Valacyclovir
This antiviral medication is indicated for managing herpes infections but does not address bacterial vaginosis.
(Choice B)
Nitrofurantoin
This antibiotic is often used to treat urinary tract infections but is not indicated for bacterial vaginosis.
(Choice C)
Amoxicillin
Amoxicillin is primarily used for treating bacterial infections, but it's not the drug of choice for bacterial vaginosis.
(Choice D)
Metronidazole
Metronidazole is recommended for managing bacterial vaginosis, characterized by 'clue cells' identified in the microscopic evaluation of the discharge. It's routinely prescribed as oral tablets or topical gel. This medication is generally safe and effective during pregnancy.
(Choice E)
Clindamycin
Clindamycin is an effective alternative treatment for bacterial vaginosis and can be used during pregnancy. However, metronidazole is preferred as first-line therapy due to superior efficacy rates and extensive safety data in pregnancy.

pages.question:
A 42-year-old man presents to the clinic with a 4-month history of profuse watery diarrhea, averaging 10-15 bowel movements per day, which persists even during fasting. He reports associated leg cramps, fatigue, and a 15-pound unintentional weight loss. Laboratory values are shown below. Abdominal CT imaging identifies a 3 cm mass in the pancreatic tail. What is the most likely diagnosis?



WBC Count	7200 /µL
Hemoglobin	13.5 g/dL
Hematocrit	40 %
RBC Count	4.6 million/µL
Platelet Count	250000 /µL
Serum Potassium	2.5 mEq/L
Serum Sodium	140 mEq/L
Chloride	102 mEq/L
Bicarbonate (HCO3-)	14 mEq/L
Arterial pH	7.25
Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN)	15 mg/dL
Serum Creatinine	0.9 mg/dL
AST (SGOT)	28 U/L
ALT (SGPT)	32 U/L
Alkaline Phosphatase	90 U/L
Total Bilirubin	0.8 mg/dL
Stool Sodium	90 mEq/L
Stool Osmolar Gap	20 mOsm/kg
Serum VIP	150 pg/mL (normal: <75 pg/mL)
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient's clinical features, including refractory watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, metabolic acidosis, and secretory stool profile, along with an elevated VIP level and pancreatic mass, are characteristic of VIPoma. VIPoma is a neuroendocrine tumor that secretes excessive VIP, leading to secretory diarrhea, electrolyte imbalances, and reduced gastric acid secretion.
(Choice A)
Carcinoid tumor
Carcinoid tumors typically present with carcinoid syndrome (flushing, diarrhea, bronchospasm) when metastatic, but the diarrhea is usually osmotic rather than secretory. The low stool osmolar gap (20 mOsm/kg) indicates secretory diarrhea, and elevated VIP levels are not characteristic of carcinoid tumors, which secrete serotonin and other vasoactive substances.
(Choice B)
Gastrinoma
Gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome) causes diarrhea due to gastric acid hypersecretion, but this typically results in acidic, high-volume stools rather than the secretory pattern seen here. The low stool osmolar gap and normal-to-low gastric acid (implied by the clinical picture) are inconsistent with gastrinoma, and VIP levels would not be elevated.
(Choice C)
VIPoma
VIPoma causes excessive secretion of vasoactive intestinal peptide, leading to secretory diarrhea, hypokalemia, and metabolic acidosis, with confirmatory elevated VIP levels and a pancreatic mass on imaging.
(Choice D)
Somatostatinoma
Somatostatinoma inhibits gastrointestinal secretions, leading to steatorrhea, diabetes, and gallstones, but not watery secretory diarrhea or hypokalemia.
(Choice E)
Laxative abuse
Laxative abuse can cause chronic diarrhea and hypokalemia, but osmotic laxatives typically produce stool osmolar gaps >50 mOsm/kg, while stimulant laxatives may cause secretory diarrhea. However, the elevated VIP levels and pancreatic mass cannot be explained by laxative abuse, making this diagnosis inconsistent with the complete clinical picture.

pages.question: A 52-year-old man with a history of major depressive disorder is brought to the emergency department after sustaining a deep laceration to his forearm while working in his garage. He has been stable on sertraline for the past year and reports no recent depressive episodes. The wound requires irrigation and suturing under local anesthesia to prevent infection. The patient is alert, oriented to person, place, and time, and engages appropriately in conversation. He accurately describes his injury, understands the proposed procedure, its risks (such as infection or scarring), benefits (wound closure and healing), alternatives (conservative management with dressings), and expresses a clear preference to proceed with suturing. The emergency physician assesses that his decision-making appears rational and unimpaired. What is the most appropriate next step regarding informed consent for this procedure?

answers.text:
Proceed with the procedure under presumed consent as it is medically urgent
(24%)

Contact the patient's family to obtain surrogate consent due to his psychiatric history
(0%)

Request a formal psychiatric evaluation to assess capacity before proceeding
(6%)

Defer the procedure and seek a court order for treatment
(0%)

Approach the patient to obtain his consent before proceeding
(70%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient with major depressive disorder demonstrates clear decision-making capacity despite his psychiatric history. He is alert, oriented, understands his condition and treatment options, appreciates the consequences, and can make a reasoned choice. Therefore, he can provide informed consent directly. Key principles: (1) Psychiatric diagnosis alone does not equal incapacity, (2) Capacity assessment focuses on current cognitive abilities, not diagnoses, (3) Surrogate consent is only needed when capacity is absent, (4) Presumed consent applies to emergencies with incapacitated patients when no surrogate is available, (5) Psychiatric consultation for capacity assessment is not required when capacity is clinically evident.
(Choice A)
Proceed with the procedure under presumed consent as it is medically urgent
This is incorrect. Presumed consent applies only to true medical emergencies where the patient is incapacitated and no surrogate decision-maker is available. This patient has capacity to consent, and while the wound requires treatment, it is not immediately life-threatening.
(Choice B)
Contact the patient's family to obtain surrogate consent due to his psychiatric history
This is incorrect. A psychiatric diagnosis alone does not imply lack of capacity. Surrogate decision-makers are only needed when the patient lacks decision-making capacity, not simply because they have a psychiatric history.
(Choice C)
Request a formal psychiatric evaluation to assess capacity before proceeding
This is incorrect. Capacity can be assessed by the treating physician; a psychiatric consult is not required if the patient clearly demonstrates understanding and rational decision-making.
(Choice D)
Defer the procedure and seek a court order for treatment
This is incorrect. Court involvement is unnecessary when the patient has capacity and consents; it is typically used in cases of refusal without capacity or when no surrogate exists.
(Choice E)
Approach the patient to obtain his consent before proceeding
This is correct. The patient has demonstrated capacity despite his psychiatric history, so he can provide informed consent himself.

pages.question:
A 72-year-old retired miner presents to the clinic with persistent fatigue and difficulty breathing. He mentions having a persistent, productive cough and occasional wheezing. He has a 30-pack-year smoking history and denies any recent respiratory infections. On examination, his breath sounds reveal rhonchi with occasional wheezing, and there is diffused ankle edema. His oxygen saturation is 88% on room air. His chest X-ray was performed, showing bilateral increased lung volumes with a barrel-shaped chest. He's initiated on a combination inhaler therapy and given oxygen support.

The following are his lab results on admission and after seven days of treatment:



Labs	Admission	7 days later
------------------------	-----------	--------------
pH	7.34	7.30
Bicarbonate, mEq/L	29	20
Serum sodium, mEq/L	137	140
Serum potassium, mEq/L	4.5	3.3
Serum chloride, mEq/L	98	110
Blood urea nitrogen (BUN), mg/dl	26	48
Serum creatinine, mg/dl	1.0	2.2
Blood glucose, mg/dl	95	132

What is the most likely explanation for the change in this patient’s acid-base status?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient with COPD initially presents with compensated respiratory acidosis. The development of acute kidney injury (rising creatinine and BUN) leads to metabolic acidosis (falling bicarbonate), representing a mixed acid-base disorder. The renal failure is likely secondary to heart failure from cor pulmonale, demonstrating cardiorenal syndrome.
(Choice A)
Primary adrenal insufficiency
Primary adrenal insufficiency typically causes hyponatremia and hyperkalemia. This patient shows normal to high sodium (137→140) and low potassium (4.5→3.3), inconsistent with adrenal insufficiency. The acute rise in creatinine better explains the acid-base changes.
(Choice B)
Corticosteroid-induced metabolic alkalosis
Corticosteroids typically cause metabolic alkalosis through increased mineralocorticoid activity. This patient demonstrates metabolic acidosis (decreasing bicarbonate from 29 to 20 mEq/L), making corticosteroid effects an unlikely explanation.
(Choice C)
Development of ketoacidosis
Ketoacidosis is unlikely given the modest glucose elevation (95→132 mg/dL). Additionally, we cannot assess the anion gap as serum CO2/bicarbonate levels alone are insufficient to calculate it without arterial blood gas pCO2 values.
(Choice D)
Acute renal failure
This patient initially has compensated respiratory acidosis (pH 7.34, HCO3 29) from COPD. The worsening renal function (creatinine 1.0→2.2, BUN 26→48) with development of metabolic acidosis (HCO3 29→20) represents acute kidney injury, likely from heart failure/cardiorenal syndrome given the clinical context of right heart strain from COPD.
(Choice E)
Progressively worsening lung disease
While this patient has COPD with initial respiratory acidosis, the key change is the development of metabolic acidosis (HCO3 29→20) with acute renal failure, not progression of the underlying lung disease.

pages.question: In a research study, a novel serum marker is being investigated for its ability to detect early-stage ovarian cancer. Initially, the marker's positivity threshold is set at 35 U/mL. Researchers lower the threshold to 20 U/mL, and observe that the number of participants with confirmed ovarian cancer who test positive increases from 60% to 85%. Which of the following best describes the effect of this threshold change?

answers.text:
The sensitivity of the test decreased
(16%)

The sensitivity of the test remained unchanged
(10.67%)

The test's false negative rate increased
(0%)

The effect on sensitivity cannot be ascertained
(7.33%)

The sensitivity of the test increased
(66%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
Adjusting diagnostic test thresholds directly affects sensitivity and specificity. Lowering the threshold increases sensitivity by allowing more patients to test positive, including more true positives (patients with disease). In this ovarian cancer screening example, lowering the threshold from 35 to 20 U/mL increased sensitivity from 60% to 85%. However, this typically comes at the cost of decreased specificity (more false positives). The choice of threshold depends on the clinical context - screening tests often favor higher sensitivity to avoid missing disease.
(Choice A)
The sensitivity of the test decreased
Lowering the threshold allows more patients to test positive, including more true positives with cancer. This increases sensitivity (true positive rate), so this choice is incorrect.
(Choice B)
The sensitivity of the test remained unchanged
When a diagnostic threshold is changed, it directly affects how many patients test positive or negative, which necessarily changes the sensitivity. The data shows sensitivity increased from 60% to 85%, so this choice is incorrect.
(Choice C)
The test's false negative rate increased
The false negative rate — defined as FN/(FN+TP), or 1 minus sensitivity — decreases when the threshold is lowered, not increases. As sensitivity rises from 60% to 85%, the false negative rate falls correspondingly from 40% to 15%. Fewer patients with confirmed ovarian cancer are being missed by the test. This is precisely the goal of lowering a screening threshold — to reduce the number of true disease cases that go undetected.
(Choice D)
The effect on sensitivity cannot be ascertained
The data clearly demonstrates that lowering the threshold increased the percentage of cancer patients who tested positive from 60% to 85%. This directly shows increased sensitivity, making this choice incorrect.
(Choice E)
The sensitivity of the test increased
Sensitivity is defined as the proportion of individuals with the disease who test positive: TP/(TP+FN). The data directly demonstrates this — lowering the threshold from 35 to 20 U/mL increased the percentage of confirmed ovarian cancer patients who tested positive from 60% to 85%. This is by definition an increase in sensitivity. By lowering the threshold, the test requires less marker elevation to be called positive, capturing more true positives at the cost of also capturing more false positives from healthy individuals. This trade-off — increased sensitivity with decreased specificity — is the fundamental consequence of lowering any diagnostic threshold. For a screening test targeting early-stage ovarian cancer, higher sensitivity is generally desirable to minimize missed diagnoses, at the accepted cost of more false positives requiring follow-up testing.
